description: We are a team of four passionate engineering students interested in Space Technology, Artificial Intelligence, Data Science and problem-solving. Our team focuses on building practical, creative and impactful solutions using Python, Machine Learning, React and modern technologies. We are participating in NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 to explore real-world challenges and develop solutions. We welcome enthusiastic people with skills in AI/ML, Data Science, Web Development, UI/UX and research.
summary:
Earth Trend Detective is a web app that helps students and the public investigate how NASA Earth science variables are changing over time. Satellite missions and models produce decades of data, but non-experts struggle to tell a real trend from noise, and trends often differ by region.

Our tool guides users through a short detective wizard. They pick a variable (with a plain-English definition), choose a region, and select a time span. The app builds a monthly time series, removes the seasonal cycle, and fits a linear trend to calculate the rate of change. It then tests significance with the Mann-Kendall test. A p-value below 0.05 is reported as Significant. Otherwise the verdict is “Not Significant Yet”, with an explanation that a longer record may confirm the trend, rather than an error.

We use NASA MERRA-2 data through Giovanni, an Arctic sea-ice melt-season record, and RADARSAT acquisition records from the Canadian Space Agency as partner data. The app is mobile-first, includes demo examples, and uses fallback data to stay reliable. AI tools such as Claude supported our development, and our team reviewed and tested the work.
details:
Earth Trend Detective is a web app that lets students and the public act as data detectives with NASA Earth science data. Users pick a variable, choose a coverage area and time span, and the app shows what is changing, how much, and whether the change is statistically significant.

How it works: a step-by-step wizard asks a short series of questions (what are you curious about, where should we look, what time span). Each variable has a plain-English definition. The backend uses Pandas to clean the monthly time series and handle missing values, removes each calendar month's seasonal average, and fits a linear trend to give the rate of change per year. It then tests significance with the Mann-Kendall test (Hamed-Rao modified version) and reports a p-value. A p-value below 0.05 is shown as Significant. Otherwise the app shows "Not Significant Yet" and explains that a longer record may confirm the trend, rather than showing an error. Users can load preset NASA datasets or import their own Giovanni CSV. Preset data stored with the project keeps the demo working if a NASA service is slow.

Benefits and impact: the tool makes NASA data approachable for high school and college students and the public, teaches the full investigation workflow (ask, select data, visualize, quantify, test), and models honest science by separating trend from cause and treating non-significant results as useful findings.

Tools: React (Vite), Leaflet maps, charts, Python, FastAPI, Pandas, SciPy, PyMannKendall.

NASA data: NASA MERRA-2 monthly 2005 to 2025 via NASA Giovanni (2-meter air temperature, total surface precipitation, total aerosol extinction AOT 550 nm), plus an Arctic sea-ice melt-season record and CSA RADARSAT (EODMS) acquisition records as partner data. The RADARSAT sample is an emergency-response sample, so we use it for browsing acquisitions, not climate trend testing.

Creativity: a detective-style wizard, plain-English definitions, and friendly handling of non-significant results make it more approachable than a plain data portal.

Limits and next steps: the current presets are global averages, and regional extraction from Giovanni is manual. Next we will automate regional extraction, suggest variables by region type, and add more missions. We test linear trends only.
